claims.statement: Epic #388 Phase 1 ruled Topology B: `varlock proxy` runs per instance on the host's loopback — where 1Password, the keychain, gpg-agent and a YubiKey can authenticate — binds 127.0.0.1 only, and injects real values on the wire while the pod holds placeholders; the design deliberately has no `--expose` and no data-plane token (Topology B deleted both, along with the WebSocket tunnel), and the lifecycle test pins that neither `--expose` nor `--persist-ca` reappears in the spawned argv.

`src/harnessed/broker.py` is the source of record for the subsystem, and three measured varlock 1.16.1 facts shape it: `proxy start` does not daemonize (so the module spawns it detached and returns), the session id is read from `proxy status --format json` matched on the chosen port (never from `start`'s ANSI-wrapped stdout), and `varlock` is invoked with `--path <schema_dir>` rather than by cwd because the mise shim resolves the binary only inside the repo.

A broker's session is identified as the `proxy status --format json` row whose `HTTPS_PROXY` ends with `:<chosen port>` — matched on the port because it is unique per instance by construction while several sessions can share an entry path and list order is unspecified; the `HTTP_PROXY` fallback is deliberately absent because a measured session sets all six proxy vars to the same URL, making it a second code path no input can reach.

Broker startup polls `proxy status` every 0.25 s for up to 30 s (`_START_TIMEOUT`) — long enough for a cold node start on a loaded machine, short enough that a broker which will never come up fails the launch instead of hanging it — while `proxy stop`/`status` control-plane calls are bounded at 30 s (`_CONTROL_TIMEOUT`) so a hung call cannot wedge a teardown path other cleanup depends on.

`launcher._broker_start_for` starts a secrets broker ONLY when the composed schema carries a `@proxy` annotation AND `--no-secrets` was not passed; the pinned contract is that no opt-in means no varlock subprocess runs at all (spawn/status/run recorders stay empty) — capability absent, not merely unrecorded — because `varlock proxy rules` resolves values and can sit on a 1Password unlock prompt, and `varlock` off PATH also means no broker and no error.

`launchenv.proxy_schema_dirs` returns the schema dirs that opted into the proxy model in `--env-file` order (user-global `~/.config/harnessed` first, then the project), deliberately mirroring `_resolve_launch_secrets`' dir selection so the broker resolves the SAME composed set the `--env-file` path resolves — otherwise the #439 placeholder handoff would give the pod placeholders for items the broker never loaded.

The gate on starting a broker is a text test, not a parse: `_schema_declares_proxy` reads `.env.schema` and matches the annotation regex `@proxy(?:Config)?\s*[(=]` (not the bare word, so prose mentioning `@proxy` does not open the gate), costing two file reads and NO subprocess; the composed-set order is global-first because `--env-file` is last-wins and the project must override the global.

`--no-secrets` reaches the backend as the `NO_SECRETS` environment variable — the same mechanism as `--no-firewall`/`NO_FIREWALL`, one mechanism for the two opt-outs; truthy spellings (`1`/`true`/`yes`, case- and whitespace-tolerant) disable the broker while falsy values (`false`/`0`/`no`/empty) deliberately do not, so a user explicitly asking for secrets never silently gets none, and the gate test pins that `--no-secrets` is a real `container_run` option flag.

A failed broker start is FATAL (#437, SPEC decision 2) — the launch aborts with `typer.Exit(1)` rather than creating a pod half-wired to a proxy that is not there, the silent half-wiring epic #388 exists to remove, which gets worse at #439 when the pod's env becomes placeholders only the broker can redeem; the failure message is fixed and value-free by construction, naming the instance and `--no-secrets` and never interpolating the exception, so a resolved value cannot reach the user.

`paths.BROKER_HOST_DOOR` (`169.254.1.1`) is the address at which a pod reaches a broker bound to the host's 127.0.0.1, and it is routable only because three places agree on the literal — paths.py owns the constant, the pod is created with pasta's `--map-host-loopback,169.254.1.1` (#437), and `catalog/base/egress-firewall.sh` ACCEPTs the address (#436) — which is why it lives in paths.py and not in any one of the three.

The firewall's broker-door rule is `require`d rather than best-effort — a failed install is a fatal, per the #429 silent-firewall history — and is deliberately NOT port-scoped: the broker port is chosen at launch and never passed to the script, so a `--dport` rule cannot be written there; narrowing it needs #437's plumbing and widening the address to a link-local CIDR is refused by #436.

The firewall-door tests execute the real `egress-firewall.sh` under bash with stubbed boundary binaries and assert on the iptables argv actually installed: the door ACCEPT appears after the `-F OUTPUT` flush and `-P OUTPUT DROP`, has no ip6tables counterpart (the address is IPv4 link-local), no link-local CIDR is ever accepted, and the only 169.254.x addresses accepted are the broker door and podman's own host-gateway.

The broker's `--map-host-loopback` composes with mcp-remote's `--host-lo-to-ns-lo` (and the plain `HARNESSED_NET` passthrough) into ONE `pasta:` `--network` value inside `mounts._mcp_remote_pasta_net_args`, because `podman pod create` accepts a single `--network` and emitting two would fail the launch; the composed form `pasta:--map-host-loopback,169.254.1.1,--host-lo-to-ns-lo` is the exact string the #388 Phase 0 spike verified with both features live, which is why the broker option is written first.

`tests/test_broker_pod_args.py` pins the composed network argv over the whole space — every broker × explicit-network × server-set combination yields at most one `--network` and at most one `pasta:` value, the invariant the composition exists to hold — and the door never appears without a broker; an explicit `HARNESSED_NET` suppresses the door with a warning that names the address and no secret, token or value.

The broker port is picked per launch from kernel-assigned ephemeral candidates (bind port 0, read the assignment) rather than hardcoded — `varlock proxy start --port` fails outright if the port is in use (measured 1.16.1), so a fixed port would make a second concurrent instance a launch failure — and picking is inherently racy and deliberately NOT locked because varlock failing loudly is cheaper than a lock held for the pod's lifetime; `--port` is still passed explicitly because the guest's `HTTPS_PROXY` must name the port before the process exists.

The ephemeral-candidate generator yields each port OUTSIDE its socket context manager — a generator suspends at its yield, so yielding inside would hand out a port the probe socket still holds, every candidate would read as taken, and `pick_port` would fail on its own default path; the default path is tested with no injected seams for exactly this reason.

`broker.start` spawns `varlock proxy start` detached (`start_new_session=True`, stdio to DEVNULL) with one repeatable `--path` per composed schema dir (up to two, so the broker resolves the same set the `--env-file` path resolves), an explicit `--port` and `--cert-dir`, polls status for the session on its port, then atomically writes the record; the cert dir defaults to a sibling of the record, starting over an existing dir is fine, and the RECORDED cert dir is asserted to equal the one passed to varlock because #438 binds that directory into the pod.

On ANY escape from the startup polling loop the spawned process is killed BEFORE any state file is written: a state file naming a dead session is merely stale (reconcile fixes it), while a live broker with no record is invisible to every cleanup path and would hold real secrets until the machine reboots — the worst orphan; the handler catches BaseException, not Exception, because the detached broker does not receive the terminal's SIGINT, so a Ctrl-C inside the up-to-30 s polling window must still kill it, as must a failure raised inside `status`.

`broker.stop` stops one session by name (`varlock proxy stop --session <id>`, never `--all`, which would kill other instances' brokers and the user's own terminals), is idempotent because teardown paths may already have run, and resolves a non-zero stop ambiguously by ASKING `status`: the record is kept when the session still lives (warning prints the manual `varlock proxy stop --session` command, naming the session id and no secret) and forgotten when the session is already gone, so `harnessed list` neither orphans a live broker nor reports a phantom forever; a corrupt record takes the early-return path and is still deleted.

`broker.reconcile(pod_exists)` is the backstop for every teardown that never ran (crashed launcher, hand-run `pod rm`, host reboot): it stops every recorded broker whose pod is gone and returns the instances reaped; it asks about the POD not the instance (the pod is what podman owns), reaps corrupt records (`all_instances` reads filenames so they are visible), keeps the record of a broker that would not die without reporting it reaped, and judges each instance independently so no branch short-circuits the sweep from reaching a later orphan.

`harnessed list`'s broker section (`_broker_report`) reconciles BEFORE reporting — a record whose pod is gone must not read as an attached broker, and the sweep doubles as periodic cleanup (issue #437 F-a) — then prints instance, session and `127.0.0.1:<port>`, which is everything the record holds so there is no redaction step; but `list` does NOT reconcile off a failed `podman ps`: on a non-zero query it warns the instance list is incomplete and returns, because a runtime that cannot be asked is not an answer and reconciling would reap every live broker.

The state record (`broker.Broker`) holds exactly five fields — instance, pod, session, port, cert_dir — so 'the state file leaks no secret' is true BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by redaction: `proxy status`'s `endpointToken` (a control-plane credential), `placeholderOverrides` and the resolved proxy env are never persisted; the lifecycle test asserts this on the raw bytes using sentinels shaped like a resolved secret, a control-plane token and a `vlk_placeholder` value, and positively that the JSON keys are exactly the five fields.

Broker records live at `$XDG_STATE_HOME/harnessed/brokers/<instance>.json` (mirroring `launcher._attach_marker`'s convention), are written atomically (temp file, then `os.replace`) so `harnessed list` and teardowns can read while a launch writes and a half-written record is never observable, and a corrupt record READS AS ABSENT — `read` swallows OSError/ValueError/KeyError/TypeError and returns None, because callers include `harnessed list` and every teardown path, with reconcile/stop then deleting the file.

`_pod_teardown` — the single choke point covering `--rm`, `--fresh`, `prune`, the stopped-leftover recreate, the stale-image recreate and the EGRESS abort path — stops the instance's broker FIRST (a host process holding live secrets must not outlive the pod) and never fatally: `_broker_stop_for` catches BaseException, not Exception, because KeyboardInterrupt is not an Exception and the `pod rm` must still run — the pod is the containment boundary, so a leaked host process is strictly better than a leaked pod, and `broker.reconcile` reaps the rest.

`_broker_stop_for` is a named wrapper rather than a bare `broker.stop(...)` call at each site because `tests/test_launch_parity` identifies capabilities by ATTRIBUTE NAME — `broker.stop(...)` inside a backend method would be indistinguishable there from the `stop` CLI command, and the ledger would record a collision instead of this capability.

The broker is started BEFORE `pod create` because the pod's network args depend on whether one exists — without a broker the pod must not be handed a route to the host's loopback it has no use for; if `pod create` then fails (Ctrl-C included, same reasoning as the EGRESS phase) the started broker is stopped before re-raising, since a broker outliving its launch is a live-secrets host process nothing will ever reap by name — worse than a leaked pod, which at least `podman ps` can see; the handle lives on the backend instance (`self.broker`, set at BOUNDARY, None when the launch gets none), not in `LaunchSpec`.

The launch-parity ledger records `_broker_start_for`, `proxy_schema_dirs` and `_broker_stop_for` as CONTAINER_ONLY by nature, not by decision: the broker exists so a CONTAINER can hold placeholders while real values are injected on the wire from the host; a host-native launch runs the harness in the user's own session with their own credentials, there is no boundary for the broker to sit on, and varlock resolves natively there already ('host: n/a (native varlock)' in the epic's backend matrix); adding such a call to `launch` without wiring it into `_launch_host` or recording a reason fails the test.

A runtime that does not use pods gets a note and resolved env instead of a half-wired broker: the door is a pasta option on `pod create`, so with no pods there is no way to deliver `169.254.1.1` into the container, and starting a broker would produce exactly the half-wired state `--no-secrets` exists to avoid — so the launch says so and resolves secrets into the container env as before.

`broker.py` reports through launcher's shared console, so it is listed in `tests/test_module_boundaries.py::EXTRACTED` (with the note that it never lived in launcher.py) and is barred from importing launcher — dependencies point INTO the modules and never back out, enforced by AST over parsed imports at any nesting depth.

Three test modules are the broker's contracts, and none spawns a real broker — which would resolve real secrets from a real 1Password — because every varlock interaction goes through the injected `spawn`/`status`/`run`/`kill` seams: `test_broker_launch_gate` pins no-opt-in-means-no-varlock-subprocess-at-all and fail-fatal; `test_broker_lifecycle` pins command order, teardown and the no-leak sentinels; `test_broker_pod_args` pins the composed network argv. No test in the repo starts a pod, so a packet crossing the pasta route is outside their reach.
